# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–6 (Complete and Final – Updated 72)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer and autumn of first year; winter of first year; Vauxhall evening during spring of first year; spring of second year; summer of second year (current narrative point); narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford, Chiswick Mall, Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London, Southampton Row, Vauxhall, Exeter 'Change, India (Boggley Wollah, Ramgunge, Budgebudge, Calcutta, Dumdum), Forty Thieves theatre, King's 14th regiment post, Highbury Barn, Covent Garden Market, Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, Bedford tavern, Thames Street (City), Royal Gardens, Quenwick, Wilhaven, St. George's Hanover Square, Lambeth Palace, Cheltenham, Great Gaunt Street, Queen's Crawley (Hants), Mudbury, Gaunt Square, Mansion House, Oxford Street, Swallow Street, Cambridge, Leakington, Squashmore, Bethesda Chapel Liverpool, Naples, Paris, Eton, Pumpernickel, Strasburg, Crawley parish, Yarlton, Quashimaboo, Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Roxby, Wapshot Hall, Christchurch, Rectory House

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Married with infant son; established pattern of two yearly visits to Grange; Dorothea's life mixed result of young, noble impulse; finely touched spirit with fine issues though not widely visible

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- Inhabit Stone Court in white-haired placidity; Fred becomes distinguished county farmer with work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding"; gradually acquired Stone Court ownership; three boys only, youngest resembles grandfather

**Rebecca Sharp (Miss Becky)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background**: Age nineteen; father was artist/drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's academy (clever, prone to debt/taverns, beat wife/daughter when drunk, died after third delirium tremens); mother was French opera-girl; claims descent from Entrechats family of Gascony (MR. PITT CRAWLEY BELIEVES her mother was a Montmorency—FACT CONFIRMED by Rebecca's ancestry research with D'Hozier's dictionary); had dismal precocity of poverty
- **Appearance**: Small, slight, pale, sandy-haired with large odd attractive eyes; white slender fingers
- **Accomplishments**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent; skilled musician, linguist, artist; sings better than Amelia
- **Character**: Determined to make plans for future; never blushed since age eight; capable of calculated charm; observant of family patterns; finds devotional practices ridiculous
- **Joseph Sedley Romance Campaign**: Upon learning of his wealth, determined to marry him; invited by Amelia; won over entire household; left alone with him in drawing-room; occupied knitting green silk purse; Joseph began eloquent speech "O Miss Sharp, how--" but stopped when music ended; continued presenting nosegays; Rebecca refused his request to sing citing low spirits; Joseph seated tete-a-tete with hands bound in green silk web; Rebecca thought "I might go farther, and fare worse"
- **At Vauxhall**: Took Jos's arm; everyone expected marriage announcement; lost themselves in solitary walk; at Moscow panorama, rude fellow treading on foot caused her to fall into Joseph's arms; at supper during inebriation, Jos clasped her round waist shouting "Stop, my dearest diddle-diddle-darling"; Rebecca started but could not get away hand
- **After Vauxhall**: George Osborne pushed Jos back into seat; Jos never came; household turned against Rebecca; Blenkinsop reported Rebecca reading Mrs. Sedley's letters and accessing trinket boxes; Pinner suspected Rebecca had taken Amelia's white ribbing; entire household (except Amelia) agreed Rebecca should depart; accepted Amelia's generous presents; received purse from Mr. Sedley; kissing his hand, asked him to consider her kind protector
- **Journey to Queen's Crawley**: Immediately counted guineas and began planning; at Leakington (heavy rain), forced outside coach as Sir Pitt is proprietor; rode outside in rain; young Cantab sheltered her kindly; guard and young man knew Sir Pitt well, called him "old screw"; carriage and four at Mudbury arrived; made entrance in state through mile-long avenue with lodge-gate having serpent and dove pillars (Crawley arms supporters)
- **First Evening**: Sir Pitt in night-cap and dressing-gown seized her candle, said "No candles after eleven o'clock, Miss Becky"; called her "pretty little hussy"; threatened to come for candle every night unless she's in bed at eleven; two bloodhounds let loose at night (Gorer killed a man; Aroarer too old to bite, formerly Flora)
- **First Dinner**: Came down with two pupils (Rose and Violet, thin insignificant, ages ten and eight); wore Amelia's muslin gown; to be treated as family except on company days; at dinner Rebecca served soup on silver soup plates with mouton aux navets; ale and water in wine-glasses for young ladies; after dinner, jug of hot water with case-bottle of rum placed before Sir Pitt; Rebecca and pupils served three little glasses of wine; Lady Crawley had bumper; Rebecca offered choice between sermons or pamphlet on corn-laws
- **Governess Duties**: Recognizes Lady Crawley (Rosa) is indolent, void of character, unnecessary to cultivate her goodwill; directs chief attention to rest of family; treats Rosa with cool respect but focuses on others; does not pester young brains with too much learning; uses extensive library at Queen's Crawley (works from Walpole Crawley's Tape and Sealing Wax Office period); contains considerable French and English light literature from last century
- **With Miss Rose Crawley**: Reads together delightful French and English works—Dr. Smollett, Henry Fielding, Monsieur Crebillon the younger, Monsieur de Voltaire; reads "Humphrey Clinker"; reads French plays while claiming to Mr. Crawley it's for acquiring French idiom; compliments Mr. Crawley on his French proficiency
- **With Miss Violet Crawley**: Violet has rude boisterous tastes; knows where hens lay eggs; climbs trees to rob nests; rides young colts; discovers jam-pot haunts; engages in battles with Rose; Rebecca promises not to tell of peccadilloes if Violet will be good and love her governess
- **With Sir Pitt**: Plays backgammon with him (Mr. Pitt criticized this as godless amusement); excused herself by claiming her dear mother used to play same game with Count de Trictrac and Abbe du Cornet; Mr. Pitt warned her about propriety
- **With Mr. Pitt Crawley**: Shows respectful obedience; consults him on French passages she cannot understand; accepts his aid in profane literature; shows interest in his Quashimaboo-Aid Society speech and malt pamphlet; affected to tears by his evening discourses; says "Oh, thank you, sir" with sighs and upward looks to heaven, earning handshakes; Mr. Crawley believes "Blood is everything" and congratulates himself on how she understands his words; believes her awakened by his words; thinks himself too fine for common people; believes her mother was a Montmorency
- **Current Status**: Has "come round" everybody (FACT—per Mrs. Crawley's reports to Rectory); writes Sir Pitt's letters, does his business, manages his accounts; has upper hand of whole house—my lady, Mr. Crawley, the girls and all; Mrs. Bute Crawley declares she is artful hussy with dreadful designs in view

**Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Financial History**: Estate never recovered from heavy fine on Walpole Crawley (first baronet) for peculation in Tape and Sealing Wax Office; Walpole was jolly, alieni appetens, sui profusus; in Walpole's day cellars filled with burgundy, kennels with hounds, stables with gallant hunters; now such horses go to plough or Trafalgar Coach
- **Character and Behavior**: Though boor, was stickler for dignity at home; seldom drove out without four horses; though dined off boiled mutton, had always three footmen to serve it; old, stumpy, short, vulgar, very dirty man in old clothes and shabby gaiters; smoking horrid pipe; shining bald head, leering red face, twinkling grey eyes, mouth perpetually on grin; country accent pronouncing avenue as "EVENUE" and nothing as "NOTHINK"; swears great deal; incessantly discusses himself; could not spell and did not care to read; had habits and cunning of boor
- **Financial Practices**: Has almost invincible repugnance to paying anybody; could only be brought by force to discharge debts; mere payment of creditors cost Baronet several hundreds yearly; savage pleasure in making poor wretches wait; said "What's the good of being in Parliament if you must pay your debts?"; position as senator useful to him
- **Parliamentary Position**: High sheriff; rode in golden coach; great ministers courted him; had higher place in Vanity Fair than most brilliant genius or spotless virtue
- **Family Relations**: From first marriage to Griselda/Grizzel (sixth daughter of Mungo Binkie, Lord Binkie); owes son Mr. Pitt Crawley sum of money from jointure of his mother which he finds inconvenient to pay (this monetary arrangement causes Mr. Pitt's hold over his affections)

**Mr. Pitt Crawley (Eldest Son)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Character and Manner**: Pale, thin, ugly, silent; thin legs, no chest; hay-coloured whiskers and straw-coloured hair; in full dress pompous as undertaker; very picture of sainted mother Griselda of house of Binkie; very earnest; high-bred propriety and respectfulness; seldom spoke to stepmother Rosa, but when did so with powerful respect; never let her quit apartment without rising stately to open door and making elegant bow
- **School Experience**: At Eton called "Miss Crawley"; younger brother Rawdon licked him violently; though parts not brilliant, made up by meritorious industry; never known to be subject to punishment during eight years
- **Career**: Prepared for public life through patronage of grandfather Lord Binkie; studied ancient and modern orators with assiduity; speaking unceasingly at debating societies; had fine flux of words; never advanced sentiment or opinion not perfectly trite and stale, supported by Latin quotation; failed despite mediocrity; did not get prize poem friends said he sure of; became Private Secretary to Lord Binkie; appointed Attache to Legation at Pumpernickel (filled with perfect honour, brought home despatches of Strasburg pie); remained ten years Attache (several years after Lord Binkie's demise); gave up diplomatic service in disgust due to slow advancement
- **Return to England**: Turned country gentleman; wrote pamphlet on Malt on returning; took strong part in Negro Emancipation question; became friend of Mr. Wilberforce; had famous correspondence with Reverend Silas Hornblower on Ashantee Mission; gave speech at Quashimaboo-Aid Society; in London during Parliament session, in May for religious meetings; in country magistrate and active visitor among destitute of religious instruction; said to be paying addresses to Lady Jane Sheepshanks (Lord Southdown's third daughter); Lady Jane's sister Lady Emily wrote "The Sailor's True Binnacle" and "The Applewoman of Finchley Common"
- **Religious Activities at Queen's Crawley**: Subjected servants to devotional exercises; brought father Sir Pitt to join; patronized Independent meeting-house in Crawley parish (to indignation of uncle the Rector, delight of Sir Pitt, who went once or twice); occasioned violent sermons at Crawley parish church directed at Baronet's Gothic pew; honest Sir Pitt did not feel force of discourses as he always took nap during sermon-time; old lady (Miss Crawley) declined to hear his hour's evening lecture; when she came to Queen's Crawley alone, he obliged to pretermit usual devotional exercises
- **Political Ambition**: Very earnest for nation and Christian world that old gentleman should yield up his place in Parliament; Sir Pitt constantly refused; both too prudent to give up fifteen hundred a year from second seat (then filled by Mr. Quadroon with carte blanche on Slave question); family estate much embarrassed; income from borough of great use to house
- **Proud of French Skills**: As diplomatist, exceedingly proud of skill in French language; not little pleased with compliments on proficiency

**Rawdon Crawley (Younger Son)** [CHARACTER INTRODUCED]
- **Background**: From Sir Pitt's first marriage to Griselda/Grizzel; at Eton licked brother Pitt violently; at college and in army had debts paid by Miss Crawley (half-sister) once or twice
- **Character and Lifestyle**: Perfect and celebrated "blood," or dandy about town; expert in boxing, rat-hunting, fives court, and four-in-hand driving (fashion of British aristocracy); belonged to household troops around Prince Regent (had not shown valour in foreign service); had already fought three bloody duels (apropos of play, of which he was immoderately fond), giving ample proofs of contempt for death; had great contempt for establishment at Queen's Crawley; seldom came there except when aunt Miss Crawley paid annual visit
- **Relationship with Miss Crawley**: This old lady took fancy to him when boy, sent him to Cambridge (in opposition to brother at Oxford); when requested by authorities to quit after two years residence, she bought him commission in Life Guards Green; she almost adopted him; disliked elder nephew Mr. Pitt exceedingly, despised him as milksop; silly, romantic Miss Crawley never horrified at his courage, always paid debts after his duels, would not listen to whispered word against his morality; "He will sow his wild oats," she would say, "and is worth far more than that puling hypocrite of a brother of his"
- **Current Status**: Known to come in for bulk of Miss Crawley's seventy-thousand-pound property

**Miss Crawley (Unmarried Half-Sister)**
- **Background and Character**: Inherited large fortune from mother; object of great respect when came to Queen's Crawley, had balance at banker's which would have made her beloved anywhere; old lady, silly and romantic; disliked Mr. Pitt exceedingly, despised him as milksop; became very attached to Rawdon when he was boy
- **Financial Position**: Possesses seventy thousand pounds; has almost adopted Rawdon; signified intention of leaving inheritance between Sir Pitt's second son (Rawdon) and family at Rectory; preferred security of funds to lending on mortgage to Sir Pitt
- **Lifestyle and Views**: Lives with atheists and Frenchmen (per Mr. Pitt's description); declined to hear Mr. Pitt's evening lecture on devotion; when came to Queen's Crawley alone, he obliged to pretermit usual devotional exercises

**Reverend Bute Crawley (Rector, Uncle to Mr. Pitt)**
- **Appearance and Character**: Tall, stately, jolly, shovel-hatted man; far more popular in his county than Baronet his brother; at college pulled stroke-oar in Christchurch boat; thrashed all best bruisers of the "town"; carried taste for boxing and athletic exercises into private life
- **Social Activity**: Not a fight within twenty miles at which he was not present, nor race, coursing match, regatta, ball, election, visitation dinner, nor good dinner in whole county but he found means to attend it; could be seen at Fuddleston, Roxby, Wapshot Hall, great lords of county with whom he was intimate; had fine voice; sang "A southerly wind and a cloudy sky"; gave "whoop" in chorus with general applause; rode to hounds in pepper-and-salt frock; one of best fishermen in county
- **Family Conflict**: Mrs. Bute Crawley is his wife; refused to visit Rosa (Lady Crawley), saying would never give pas to tradesman's daughter; brother Sir Pitt had better of him in innumerable family transactions

**Other Characters**
- **Mrs. Bute Crawley**: Rector's wife; refused to visit Rosa; bright eyes spy out everything at Hall; doings at Hall great food for conversation at Rectory; reports Rebecca is artful hussy with dreadful designs
- **Mr. Horrocks** (Butler): Serves at meals; laughed with Sir Pitt; taught to say "My lady is served"; insists on handing her ladyship in to dinner
- **Mr. Hodson** (Hind from Mudbury): Estate manager; Sir Pitt's representative in farming matters and cracking whip at vagrant boys
- **George Osborne, William Dobbin, Joseph Sedley, Miss Amelia Sedley, Lady Jane Sheepshanks, Lady Emily, Mr. Wilberforce, Reverend Silas Hornblower, Mr. Quadroon**
- **Walpole Crawley**: First baronet; impeached for peculation in Tape and Sealing Wax Office; received heavy fine
- **Lord Binkie**: Grandfather of Mr. Pitt Crawley; deceased (lamented)
- **Background characters with scattered narrative mentions**: Ridan, Nyrine Wexwood, Thiena, Pebin Wexwood, Ridette Lindson, Ellan Lindner, Wevie Lindner, Conar Hollett, Thidrek, Nyvie Hollett (died of long wasting sickness, buried at Mirecombe), Madan Brackwood

## Critical Facts and Status
- Narrator reflects on Vanity Fair as "a very vain, wicked, foolish place, full of all sorts of humbugs and falsenesses and pretensions"
- Parliamentary seat at Queen's Crawley worth fifteen hundred a year; family estate much embarrassed; income from borough of great use to house
- Rebecca has successfully gained upper hand of entire Queen's Crawley household—her accomplishment as governess complete within summer of second year
- Money transactions between brothers create silent battles for reversionary spoil in Vanity Fair; Rawdon set to inherit bulk of Miss Crawley's seventy-thousand-pound property
- Narrator warns that accounts of Mr. Pitt Crawley's employment are not caricatures; narrator states "I, for my part, have known a five-pound note to interpose and knock up a half century's attachment between two brethren"
